Class GraphCanvasModel

java.lang.Object
ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphCanvasModel
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable
public class GraphCanvasModel extends Object implements Serializable
What the editor canvas holds: one drawing, plus the frames that mark out the Petri-objects in it and the places that were joined across those frames.

The drawing stays a single net, the way it always was — elements, arcs, selection, undo and copy all work on it unchanged. Which Petri-object an element belongs to is what its frame explicitly claims (claim(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame, ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement)), not where it happens to sit - so dragging a frame across the canvas can never quietly pick up something it passes over. An arc that crosses between two objects' elements is therefore not an arc of any net but a link between them, and toObjModel() is where that reading happens.

Ownership is single-valued and this class is its only writer. claim(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame, ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement) releases whatever held an element before claiming it for a new frame, so ownerOf(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement) can never find two claimants and has no tie to break. That used to be a convention spread over six callers of GraphObjectFrame.addMember, and the frame a user had just created could therefore hold nothing at all: ownerOf answered with whichever frame came first in canvas order, so the new one was invisible to every reader.

A frame can sit inside another frame - nesting one Petri-object in another. That is a frame-to-frame relation (nest(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame, ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame), enclosingOf(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame)), laid on top of the flat getFrames() list rather than replacing it, because that list's order is what indexes objects in toObjModel(), in the PNML document and in the statistics formulas. A nested object is consequently an ordinary sibling object of the model it exports to, which is exactly what the web editor does with the same relation.

Anything drawn outside every frame still simulates: it is gathered into one last, unnamed Petri-object, so a plain net drawn without any frame is a model of one object.

    • GraphCanvasModel

      public GraphCanvasModel(GraphCanvasModel other)
      Deep-copies another canvas: a fully independent net, frames whose membership is translated onto the new net's own element instances, and fusions rebuilt the same way — nothing here is shared with other, so mutating the copy (running a simulation on it, editing it) can never reach back into other or vice versa.

      This is the piece a plain net-only snapshot (new GraphPetriNet(canvas.getNet())) cannot give you: the net alone has no notion of Petri-object frames, so restoring from one always came back as loose elements with every frame gone — this is the fix for that.

      Parameters:
      other - the canvas to copy

      public List<GraphObjectFrame> getFrames()
      Returns:
      every frame on the canvas at every depth, in creation order - nesting does not change this list or its order. That order is load-bearing: toObjModel() indexes objects by position in it, the PNML writer keys its pages by that index and the statistics formulas resolve an object the same way, which is also why nesting needs no change to any of them.

    • placesOf

      public List<GraphPetriPlace> placesOf(GraphObjectFrame frame)
      The places belonging to one Petri-object, in the order the model addresses them by.

      The same order links are written and read in - "the n-th place of the object's page" - so an index into this list means the same thing here, in a saved document, and across two objects stamped from one net. That is what lets a link be replicated across a group: the place at index i of one member is the place at index i of every other.

      Parameters:
      frame - the object, which may be null for the places belonging to no object
      Returns:
      its places, in canvas order

    • removeDanglingGroupMembers

      public void removeDanglingGroupMembers()
      Drops members that are no longer on the canvas, and groups that no longer hold enough objects to be one.

      Called wherever removeDanglingFusions() is, and for the same reason: deleting an object cannot be expected to know every record that mentioned it. A group that has fallen to a single member is dissolved rather than kept - one object stamped from a template is just an object, and leaving a group of one would draw a stack around it and offer to replicate a connector across a group of one.

    • absorbStructureOf

      public void absorbStructureOf(GraphCanvasModel other, Map<GraphElement,GraphElement> oldToNew)
      Takes on another canvas's structure - its Petri-objects, the nest between them and the places they share - after that canvas's drawing has already been merged into this one's.

      Merging a net copies every element rather than adopting the instances, so that two documents opened one after the other cannot collide over an id. Everything that pointed at the originals therefore has to be rebuilt against the copies, and this is where that happens: a frame's membership, a fusion's two halves and the frames it is anchored to. Appending other's own frames and fusions instead - which is what this used to be - left them referring to instances that were never put on the canvas. The visible result was a document whose every element came out unowned: the objects were drawn as empty rooms around a net that belonged to nobody, Ctrl+A picked up all of it as free elements, dragging that selection asked to move every element into "a different Petri-object", and the shared-place links stayed behind at their old coordinates because both of their ends were off-canvas ghosts.

      Parameters:
      other - the canvas whose structure to take on
      oldToNew - that canvas's elements mapped to the copies this canvas's net now holds, as GraphPetriNet.mergeGraphNet reports it; an element missing from the map is one the merge did not copy, and whatever referred to it is dropped rather than left dangling

    • frameAt

      public GraphObjectFrame frameAt(Point2D point)
      Parameters:
      point - a point on the canvas
      Returns:
      the innermost frame whose rectangle contains the point, or null. The deepest nesting level wins, and among frames at the same level the later one in canvas order does. A hit test for clicks and menus; it says nothing about which object an element belongs to, see ownerOf(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement).

      Deepest-first matters because it is the same rule ownerOf(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement) follows: a nested object's own element belongs to the nested object, so a click inside the nested object's rectangle has to resolve to it too. The two used to break an overlap tie in opposite directions, which is what made a frame drawn inside another frame inconsistent to reason about at all.

    • ownerOf

      public GraphObjectFrame ownerOf(GraphElement element)
      Parameters:
      element - an element of the drawing
      Returns:
      the frame that claims it (GraphObjectFrame.hasMember(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement)), or null when no frame does, which makes it one of the free elements. Always the DIRECT owner: an element inside a nested object belongs to that nested object, never to its parent. Ask membersOfSubtree(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame) for the parent's outward-facing content.

      A shared place used to short-circuit this and answer with whichever frame owned it when the fusion was made. That was stale twice over: the two halves are no longer moved on top of each other, so there is nothing for the fusion to disambiguate, and a removed frame kept answering forever.

    • refreshFusionOwners

      public void refreshFusionOwners()
      Re-reads which frame owns each half of every shared place. A fusion used to freeze its two owners at join time, so ungrouping the owning object, dragging a half elsewhere or removing a frame left it anchored to a frame no longer on the canvas: it kept drawing a line to a ghost and could never fall back to the coincident-ring form.

    • framesParentFirst

      public List<GraphObjectFrame> framesParentFirst()
      Returns:
      every frame ordered so a parent always comes before its children - the order to paint a nest in, since a child has to be drawn over the parent it sits inside. A frame whose parent is missing from the canvas, or which is caught in a cycle, surfaces at the top level rather than being dropped: a frame the user can see has to be painted whatever state its parent pointer got into.

    • releaseMembers

      public void releaseMembers(GraphObjectFrame removed)
      Called when a frame is removed: what it held does not vanish along with it, it moves one level out. Its elements go to the object that enclosed it, becoming free when nothing did, and the objects nested inside it are re-nested onto that same enclosing object.

      This used to be decided by geometry - the released elements fell to whichever other frame's rectangle happened to cover them. With nesting that is actively wrong: removing an outer frame handed its whole net to the frame drawn inside it, which is the opposite of what removing the outer object means.

      Parameters:
      removed - the frame that was just taken off the canvas

    • fusionsOf

      public List<GraphPlaceFusion> fusionsOf(GraphPetriPlace place)
      Every reference link this place takes part in, in either role.

      Returns a list rather than one link, and replaced a fusionOf that returned the first match, because a place may now be the source of any number of links. Answering with whichever one happened to be found first was correct only while a place could be in at most one, and would have silently ignored the rest the moment that stopped being true.

      Parameters:

      Returns:
      its links, newest last; empty if it takes part in none

    • connectorOf

      public List<GraphPlaceFusion> connectorOf(GraphPlaceFusion link)
      The connector a link belongs to: every link joining the same two Petri-objects.

      A connector is the technique's own name for the whole set of shared places between one pair of objects, written connector(o_u, o_v) = {(o_u.net.p_b, o_v.net.p_a)}. Two objects sharing three places are joined by one connector of three place identifications, not by three unrelated links, and treating it as one thing is what lets the pair be reasoned about - and detached - as a unit.

      Derived, never stored. A connector is entirely determined by which objects the existing links run between, so keeping a second record of it could only ever be a record that disagrees; this is the same reason the two-way arc pairing and the linked-place mark are both re-derived rather than maintained.

      A link with an end belonging to no object is a connector of its own. The concept joins two Petri-objects, and loose places are not one - bundling every loose link into a single enormous "no-object" connector would be an artefact of saying null equals null.

      Parameters:
      link - one of this canvas's links
      Returns:
      the links of its connector, in declaration order, including link itself; a single-element list when nothing else joins the same pair

    • portsOf

      public List<FramePort> portsOf(GraphObjectFrame frame)
      Computes the port markers a frame shows on its border: one per place and one per transition it owns, each sitting on whichever side of the frame — left, right or bottom, never the header side on top — is closest to where the element itself actually is, so a port reads as "this element, right about here" rather than an arbitrary slot.

      Ports are what a locked object is connected to other objects through, since its own elements can no longer be dragged directly on the shared canvas. Nothing about a port is stored — it is derived fresh from the frame's current bounds and its current elements every time, so moving or resizing a frame, or editing its net, keeps the ports in step without any bookkeeping of its own.

      One port per element of membersOfSubtree(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame), not just per direct member: from outside, a nest is one object, so a collapsed parent still shows where everything inside it - including everything its nested objects hold - can be connected. For an object with nothing nested in it that is exactly its own members, so nothing changes.

      Parameters:
      frame - the object to compute ports for
      Returns:
      the frame's ports, places first then transitions, both in net order

    • portAt

      public FramePort portAt(Point2D point)
      Parameters:
      point - a point on the canvas
      Returns:
      the port under that point, across every frame, or null. While an object's content is actually shown (GraphObjectFrame.isContentShown()), a point on the real place or transition itself also resolves to that element's port — its circle is not drawn there in that case, but the port it stands for is still exactly what a link from it should be, so there is no reason a locked element's own drawing should not be draggable the same way its port would be

    • toObjModel

      public GraphPetriObjModel toObjModel()
      Reads the canvas as a Petri-object model.

      Objects come out in frame order, with everything drawn outside every frame gathered into a last unnamed object. An output arc whose ends sit in different objects becomes a transition-to-place link, and a shared place becomes a place fusion.

      An input arc may not cross an object boundary: a transition takes its input places from its own Petri-object only, so such an arc is refused rather than turned into a link. The canonical drawing is a shared place plus an ordinary arc inside the object that owns the transition, which means exactly the same thing.

      Returns:
      the model the canvas describes
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the canvas has nothing on it
      IllegalArgumentException - if an input arc runs from a place of one object to a transition of another

    • fromObjModel

      public static GraphCanvasModel fromObjModel(GraphPetriObjModel model)
      Lays a Petri-object model out on one canvas: a frame per object, its net inside, and the links restored as arcs crossing frame borders or as shared places.

      The nest between objects is restored too, in a second pass once every frame exists. A model carries it as each object's parent index, which a document states by writing a child object's <page> inside its parent's, the way ISO/IEC 15909-2 states a hierarchy of pages.

      Parameters:
      model - the model to show
      Returns:
      the canvas that draws it

    • framesInOrder

      public List<GraphObjectFrame> framesInOrder()
      Returns:
      the frames, in the order that indexes the objects they mark out
